label: Laser light
summary: Laser diodes from DVD and Blu-ray writers, laser pointers and laser cutters can burn the retina faster than you can blink, causing permanent blind spots. Many lasers are invisible: CD drives, fibre-optic links and some sensors use infrared, and CO2 and fibre laser cutters use invisible beams that burn skin and start fires. Blue diode engravers are visible but just as dangerous.
signs: Optical drives (DVD writers have the strongest diodes), barcode scanners and laser printers
Warning stickers with a starburst symbol, or Class 3B or Class 4
do: Treat every salvaged laser diode as able to blind you
Power diodes only through a current-limited driver
Point the beam at a dark, matte, non-flammable target such as brick or concrete, never at anything shiny
Wear laser goggles rated for that wavelength and power when testing
Keep other people and animals out of the room
dont: Don't look into the beam or along it, even briefly
Don't look at reflections from glass, metal or water
Don't assume a laser is off because you can't see a beam
Don't point a laser at people, animals, vehicles or aircraft
Don't trust sunglasses: they don't protect against lasers
Don't open a CO2 laser cutter's tube or power supply until it's unplugged and discharged: it runs on tens of thousands of volts
ppe: Laser safety glasses rated for the wavelength: about 405 nm (Blu-ray), 450–460 nm (blue diode engravers), 532 nm (green pointers), 650 nm (DVD), 780 nm (CD), 1,064 nm (fibre lasers, and the hidden infrared from cheap green pointers), or 10,600 nm (CO2 cutters)
firstAid: There is no first aid for a laser eye injury
A blind spot, an afterimage that doesn't fade, or blurred vision after exposure needs an eye examination
Skin burns: cool under cool running water for 20 minutes
